decisions.quote:
Eriksson and Coultas (2009) found no
     conformity bias using quizzes in which the answers were not objectively fixed as correct or incorrect (e.g., belief,
     preference, and norm). We replicated their experiment using questions with fixed answers. In this study (N = 120),
     after participants answered “yes/no” to 14 questions, they were informed of the four patterns of the distribution of
     the other nine participants’ responses (9, 6, 3, 0 participants said “yes”). Then, participants completed the same
     questions again. The results showed that conformity bias was observed. We discuss the inconsistency of the results
     between the previous study and our study.
decisions.reason: This study is a completed new-sample replication of Eriksson and Coultas (2009, DOI: 10.1556/jep.7.2009.1.3). Eriksson and Coultas (2009) found no conformity bias (reporting negative D* values / an inverse S-shaped nonconformist bias on attitude/belief/norm questions). Re-testing their paradigm with N = 120 participants across both objective questions (9 items) and attitude questions (5 items), Fujikawa et al. (2024) found positive D* values (conformity bias) across all items (objective 95% CI [0.93, 1.54]; attitude 95% CI [0.22, 0.88]) and better AIC fit for the conformity-bias model than the unbiased proportional model in both question types, explicitly concluding in both the Abstract and Discussion (p. 510, '先行研究との不一致') that their results are inconsistent with Eriksson and Coultas (2009). Per the codebook, finding an effect where the original found none (and explicitly stating inconsistency with the original finding) codes as 'failed'.
